teaching.hint: Which bit positions must be set in every array entry for their common AND to retain each set bit of x?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Every array entry must be a supermask of x. The zero positions of x are free positions into which the bits of 0,1,2,... can be placed in order, yielding the supermasks in increasing numeric order.
solution_outline.approach: Take n-1 in binary and place its bits from low to high into the zero-bit positions of x, leaving every one-bit of x set. Return this nth supermask.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: As free bit positions are filled from low to high, the constructed value has x's fixed bits and the already consumed low bits of n-1 in the corresponding free positions. This mapping preserves numeric order.
solution_outline.correctness: Any valid entry must contain all one-bits of x, so an increasing valid array needs n distinct supermasks; its end is at least the nth smallest. The mapping from ordinary nonnegative integers to supermasks preserves order. Its first n outputs start with x, so their AND is exactly x, and the nth output attains the lower bound.
solution_outline.complexity: O(log n + log x) bit positions examined and O(1) auxiliary space. The result can require 64-bit storage.
solution_outline.pitfall: Setting only the bits of x in the answer misses the need to reserve distinct larger entries for a strictly increasing array.

common_wrong_turns: Assume each zero-bit position can only be used once across the array
Build arbitrary supermasks without proving the endpoint minimum
source_fidelity_notes: The strict increase, positive values, global AND requirement, n and x bounds, and endpoint-only output were retained; 64-bit growth was clarified.
